{{Short description|Theorem on orthonormal sequences}}
In [[mathematics]], especially [[functional analysis]], '''Bessel's inequality''' is a statement about the coefficients of an element <math>x</math> in a [[Hilbert space]] with respect to an [[orthonormal]] [[sequence]]. The inequality is named for [[Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel|F. W. Bessel]], who derived a special case of it in 1828.<ref name="EoM">{{Cite web|url=https://www.encyclopediaofmath.org/index.php/Bessel_inequality|title = Bessel inequality - Encyclopedia of Mathematics}}</ref>

Conceptually, the inequality is a generalization of the [[Pythagorean theorem]] to infinite-dimensional spaces. It states that the "[[Energy (signal processing)|energy]]" of a vector <math>x</math>, given by <math>\|x\|^2</math>, is greater than or equal to the sum of the energies of its [[Projection (linear algebra)|projections]] onto a set of perpendicular basis directions. The value <math>|\langle x, e_k \rangle|^2</math> represents the energy contribution along a specific direction <math>e_k</math>, and the inequality guarantees that the sum of these contributions cannot exceed the total energy of <math>x</math>.

When the orthonormal sequence forms a complete [[orthonormal basis]], Bessel's inequality becomes an equality known as [[Parseval's identity]]. This signifies that the sum of the energies of the projections equals the total energy of the vector, meaning no energy is "lost." The inequality is a crucial tool for establishing the convergence of [[Fourier series]] and other series expansions in Hilbert spaces.

==Statement of the inequality==
Let <math>H</math> be a Hilbert space and let <math>e_1, e_2, \dots</math> be an orthonormal sequence in <math>H</math>. Then for any vector <math>x</math> in <math>H</math>, Bessel's inequality states:
:<math>\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\left\vert\left\langle x,e_k\right\rangle \right\vert^2 \le \left\Vert x\right\Vert^2</math>
where ⟨·,·⟩ denotes the [[inner product space|inner product]] in the Hilbert space <math>H</math>, and <math>\|\cdot\|</math> denotes the [[norm (mathematics)|norm]] induced by the inner product.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QALoZC64ea0C|title=Beginning Functional Analysis|last=Saxe|first=Karen|authorlink= Karen Saxe |date=2001-12-07|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=9780387952246|pages=82|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XF8W9W-eyrgC|title=Mathematical Analysis II|last1=Zorich|first1=Vladimir A.|last2=Cooke|first2=R.|date=2004-01-22|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=9783540406334|pages=508–509|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LBZEBAAAQBAJ|title=Foundations of Signal Processing|last1=Vetterli|first1=Martin|last2=Kovačević|first2=Jelena|last3=Goyal|first3=Vivek K.|date=2014-09-04|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=9781139916578|pages=83|language=en}}</ref>

The terms <math>\langle x,e_k\rangle</math> are the [[Fourier coefficient]]s of <math>x</math> with respect to the sequence <math>(e_k)</math>. The inequality implies that the series of the squared magnitudes of these coefficients converges. This allows for the definition of the vector <math>x'</math>, which is the projection of <math>x</math> onto the subspace spanned by the orthonormal sequence:
:<math>x' = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\left\langle x,e_k\right\rangle e_k</math>
Bessel's inequality guarantees that this [[series (mathematics)|series]] [[Limit of a sequence|converges]]. If the sequence <math>(e_k)</math> is a complete [[orthonormal basis]], then <math>x' = x</math>, and the inequality becomes an equality known as [[Parseval's identity]].

===Proof===
The inequality follows from the non-negativity of the norm of a vector. For any natural number <math>n</math>, let
:<math>x_n = \sum_{k=1}^n \langle x, e_k \rangle e_k</math>
This vector <math>x_n</math> is the projection of <math>x</math> onto the subspace spanned by the first <math>n</math> basis vectors. The vector <math>x-x_n</math> is orthogonal to this subspace, and thus orthogonal to <math>x_n</math> itself. By the [[Pythagorean theorem#Inner product spaces|Pythagorean theorem for inner product spaces]], we have <math>\|x\|^2 = \|x_n\|^2 + \|x-x_n\|^2</math>. The proof proceeds by computing <math>\|x - x_n\|^2</math>:
:<math>\begin{align}
0 \leq \left\| x - \sum_{k=1}^n \langle x, e_k \rangle e_k\right\|^2 &= \left\langle x - \sum_{k=1}^n \langle x, e_k \rangle e_k, \; x - \sum_{j=1}^n \langle x, e_j \rangle e_j \right\rangle \\
&= \|x\|^2 - \sum_{k=1}^n \overline{\langle x, e_k \rangle} \langle x, e_k \rangle - \sum_{j=1}^n \overline{\langle x, e_j \rangle} \langle e_j, x \rangle + \sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \overline{\langle x, e_k \rangle} \langle x, e_j \rangle \langle e_k, e_j \rangle \\
&= \|x\|^2 - \sum_{k=1}^n |\langle x, e_k \rangle |^2 - \sum_{j=1}^n |\langle x, e_j \rangle |^2 + \sum_{k=1}^n | \langle x, e_k \rangle |^2 \\
&= \|x\|^2 - \sum_{k=1}^n | \langle x, e_k \rangle |^2
\end{align}</math>
This holds for any <math>n \ge 1</math>. Since the partial sums are non-negative and bounded above by <math>\|x\|^2</math>, the series <math>\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}|\langle x,e_k\rangle|^2</math> converges and its sum is less than or equal to <math>\|x\|^2</math>.
==Fourier series==

In the theory of [[Fourier series]], in the particular case of the Fourier orthonormal system, we get if <math>f \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C} </math> has period <math>T</math>,
:<math>
  \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} \left\vert \int_0^T e^{-2 \pi i k t/T} f (t) \,\mathrm{d}t\right\vert^2 \le T \int_0^T \vert f (t)\vert^2 \,\mathrm{d}t.
</math>
In the particular case where <math>f \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} </math>, one has then 
:<math>
 \left\vert \int_0^T f (t) \,\mathrm{d}t\right\vert^2
 + 2 \sum_{n = 1}^\infty \left\vert \int_0^T \cos (2 \pi k t/T) f (t) \,\mathrm{d}t\right\vert^2
 + 2 \sum_{n = 1}^\infty \left\vert \int_0^T \sin (2 \pi k t/T) f (t) \,\mathrm{d}t\right\vert^2 \le T \int_0^T \vert f (t)\vert^2 \,\mathrm{d}t.
</math>

==Non countable case==

More generally, if <math>H</math> is a pre-Hilbert space and <math>(e_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}</math> is an orthonormal system, then for every <math>x \in H</math><ref name="EoM" />
:<math>
  \sum_{\alpha \in A}  | \langle x, e_\alpha \rangle |^2 \le \lVert x \rVert^2
</math>
This is proved by noting that if <math>F \subseteq A</math> is finite, then 
:<math>
  \sum_{\alpha \in F}  | \langle x, e_\alpha \rangle |^2 \le \lVert x \rVert^2
</math>
and then by definition of [[Series (mathematics)#Families of non-negative numbers|infinite sum]]  
:<math>
   \sum_{\alpha \in A}  | \langle x, e_\alpha \rangle |^2 = \sup \Bigl\{\sum_{\alpha \in F}  | \langle x, e_\alpha \rangle |^2 : F \subseteq A \text{ is finite}\Bigr\}
   \le \lVert x \rVert^2.
</math>
